items.prompt: State what is meant by the value of a physical quantity.
items.canonical_answer: The value of a physical quantity is its numerical magnitude together with its unit: the unit names the standard the magnitude is counted against, and the two together state the quantity.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition — a numerical magnitude together with its unit; the unit is part of the value, so a bare number states no quantity.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: understand that all physical quantities consist of a numerical magnitude and a unit

items.prompt: A learner records the length of a fence wire as 200. Explain why the record does not state a physical quantity, and how to complete it.
items.canonical_answer: The record gives a numerical magnitude with no unit. A physical quantity consists of a magnitude and a unit together, because the unit names the standard the magnitude is counted against: 200 m and 200 cm are different lengths, so the number alone is incomplete. The record is completed by adding the unit — 200 m — which then states the length.
marking_guidance: Mark 1: how the record is incomplete — a magnitude without a unit states no quantity, because the unit is part of the value.
Mark 2: how to complete it — add the unit, which names the standard counted against, and the two parts then state the length.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: understand that all physical quantities consist of a numerical magnitude and a unit

items.prompt: State one property of the unit of a physical quantity, as distinct from its numerical magnitude.
items.canonical_answer: The unit names the standard the magnitude is counted against, and it is part of the value: changing the unit changes the quantity stated, as 1.5 km and 1.5 m are different lengths.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one property of the unit — it names the standard counted against and is part of the value, unlike the magnitude, which counts how many of that standard are used.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: understand that all physical quantities consist of a numerical magnitude and a unit

items.prompt: State what is meant by a reasonable estimate of a physical quantity.
items.canonical_answer: A reasonable estimate states a magnitude with its unit, judged without measuring directly, and is expected to lie within about a power of ten of the actual value.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition — a magnitude with its unit, judged without direct measurement, expected within about a power of ten of the actual value.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: make reasonable estimates of physical quantities included within the syllabus

items.prompt: Explain how a known reference quantity helps a learner estimate the mass of a loaded minibus taxi.
items.canonical_answer: The estimate is built from a reference: an adult person has a mass of about 70 kg, and a loaded taxi carries about twenty passengers. Twenty adults come to 20 × 70 = 1400 kg, which is about 1.4 × 10³ kg for the passengers, so the taxi and its load together come to around 3 × 10³ kg. The reference anchors the power of ten, which is how the estimate is checked against a quantity of the same kind.
marking_guidance: Mark 1: how the reference anchors the estimate — a known mass of about 70 kg per person gives the starting point, because the estimate is judged against a quantity of the same kind.
Mark 2: how the total is built — 20 × 70 = 1400 kg, so about 1.4 × 10³ kg, which keeps the estimate within about a power of ten.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: make reasonable estimates of physical quantities included within the syllabus

items.prompt: State one property that a reasonable estimate of a physical quantity is expected to have.
items.canonical_answer: It lies within about a power of ten of the actual value: a magnitude with its unit, judged without measuring directly, that a reference quantity of the same kind can defend.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one property — within about a power of ten of the actual value, stated as a magnitude with its unit and judged without measuring directly.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: make reasonable estimates of physical quantities included within the syllabus

items.prompt: State the SI base quantity that the ampere is the unit of.
items.canonical_answer: Electric current. The ampere is the unit of the base quantity electric current, not the quantity itself.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the base quantity named — electric current; the ampere is its unit, which is why answering with a unit or a derived quantity does not score.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: recall the following SI base quantities and their units: mass (kg), length (m), time (s), current (A), temperature (K)

items.prompt: State one feature that distinguishes a base quantity from a derived quantity.
items.canonical_answer: A base quantity is one of the quantities the others are built from, while a derived quantity is built from base quantities through its defining equation — charge comes from current and time, so charge is derived, not base.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one distinguishing feature — base quantities are the set the others are built from; charge is derived because it is built from current and time.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: recall the following SI base quantities and their units: mass (kg), length (m), time (s), current (A), temperature (K)

items.prompt: Asked to state the SI base quantities, a learner answers: kg, A and charge. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The answer mixes units with a derived quantity, when base quantities are asked for. The kilogram and the ampere are units, not quantities; charge is a quantity, but a derived one, built from current and time. The base quantities are mass, length, time, electric current and temperature (with amount of substance completing the AS set), whose units are kg, m, s, A, K and mol. The test is whether each item in the answer is a quantity or a unit.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named, in fact two errors in one — base units given instead of base quantities, and a derived quantity (charge) given instead; the correct idea is the quantity list mass, length, time, current, temperature. Register entry MC-9702-1-01.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger; discriminates misconception register entry MC-9702-1-01.
objective_titles: recall the following SI base quantities and their units: mass (kg), length (m), time (s), current (A), temperature (K)

items.prompt: State what is meant by a derived unit.
items.canonical_answer: A derived unit is written as a product or quotient of SI base units: the newton is N = kg m s⁻², and the pascal is Pa = kg m⁻¹ s⁻².
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition — a unit written as a product or quotient of base units, with a correct example such as N = kg m s⁻².
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: express derived units as products or quotients of the SI base units and use the derived units for quantities listed in this syllabus as appropriate

items.prompt: Explain how the base units of the pascal follow from the defining equation of pressure.
items.canonical_answer: Pressure is defined by p = F/A, so its unit follows by substituting the units: force is kg m s⁻² and area is m², and dividing gives kg m⁻¹ s⁻², the pascal. The unit is read straight off the equation because each symbol is replaced by its unit and the powers simplify, which is how any derived unit is built.
marking_guidance: Mark 1: how the unit follows from the equation — p = F/A, so the unit is N/m², which in base units is kg m⁻¹ s⁻², because each symbol is replaced by its unit.
Mark 2: how the simplification works — m s⁻² divided by m² leaves m⁻¹ s⁻², so the pascal equals kg m⁻¹ s⁻².
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: express derived units as products or quotients of the SI base units and use the derived units for quantities listed in this syllabus as appropriate

items.prompt: Asked to express the joule in SI base units, a learner writes J. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The joule is itself a derived unit, so writing J leaves the conversion unfinished. Energy in base units is kg m² s⁻², from W = Fd: force is kg m s⁻² and distance is m, which multiply to kg m² s⁻². The test is whether the final unit contains base units only — kg, m, s, A, K and mol — and J alone does not.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named — a derived unit left in the answer instead of base units; the correct idea is J = kg m² s⁻², because the test is whether the final unit contains base units only. Register entry MC-9702-1-02.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger; discriminates misconception register entry MC-9702-1-02.
objective_titles: express derived units as products or quotients of the SI base units and use the derived units for quantities listed in this syllabus as appropriate

items.prompt: State one feature that every derived unit has.
items.canonical_answer: Every derived unit can be written as a product or quotient of SI base units: the watt is kg m² s⁻³, and the newton is kg m s⁻².
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one feature — expressible as a product or quotient of base units, with any correct example (N, Pa, J, W) written in base units.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: express derived units as products or quotients of the SI base units and use the derived units for quantities listed in this syllabus as appropriate

items.prompt: State what is meant by a homogeneous equation.
items.canonical_answer: An equation is homogeneous when every term in it carries the same SI base units, so the two sides can be equated and the terms added; homogeneity is necessary for a physical equation to be correct, not sufficient.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition — every term carries the same SI base units; adding that this is necessary, not sufficient, is welcome alongside the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: use SI base units to check the homogeneity of physical equations

items.prompt: The equation W = mv is proposed for the work done by a force, where m is the mass of the object moved and v is its speed. Calculate the base units of each side of the equation and state whether the equation is homogeneous.
items.canonical_answer: Work in base units: force is kg m s⁻² and distance is m, so the left side W is kg m² s⁻². The right side, mv, is the product of mass and speed, kg and m s⁻¹, which is kg m s⁻¹. The two sides differ (kg m² s⁻² against kg m s⁻¹), so the equation is not homogeneous.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: W from force kg m s⁻² times distance m, giving kg m² s⁻², and mv as kg m s⁻¹ — 1 mark for the working on both sides.
Final answer: the sides differ, so the equation is not homogeneous, with the units of both sides stated — 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: use SI base units to check the homogeneity of physical equations

items.prompt: The electrical power dissipated in a resistor is proposed as P = I²R, where I is the current and R has base units kg m² s⁻³ A⁻². Calculate the base units of each side of the equation and state whether the equation is homogeneous.
items.canonical_answer: Left side, power: the watt is J s⁻¹, and J = kg m² s⁻², so power is kg m² s⁻³. Right side: I² is A², and A² multiplied by kg m² s⁻³ A⁻² cancels to kg m² s⁻³. Both sides carry kg m² s⁻³, so the equation is homogeneous.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: the left side kg m² s⁻³ from J = kg m² s⁻² per second, and the right side A² × kg m² s⁻³ A⁻² cancelling to kg m² s⁻³ — 1 mark for the working.
Final answer: homogeneous, with the units of both sides stated — 1 mark. Matching units confirm homogeneity; they do not confirm any numerical constant.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: use SI base units to check the homogeneity of physical equations

items.prompt: An equation for the speed of a falling object is proposed as v = at², where a is its acceleration and t is the time of fall. Calculate the base units of the right side and state whether the equation is homogeneous.
items.canonical_answer: Acceleration is m s⁻² and time squared is s², so the right side is m s⁻² multiplied by s², which is m. Speed on the left is m s⁻¹. The two sides differ (m against m s⁻¹), so the equation is not homogeneous; the correct relationship uses time to the first power.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: at² in base units as m s⁻² with s², which simplifies to m — 1 mark.
Final answer: not homogeneous, because the left side carries m s⁻¹ and the right side m — 1 mark. The units of both sides decide the answer.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: use SI base units to check the homogeneity of physical equations

items.prompt: State one feature of a homogeneous equation that a homogeneity test cannot confirm.
items.canonical_answer: The test cannot confirm the numerical constants: F = 2ma is homogeneous, because a pure number carries no units, yet the equation is wrong. Homogeneity is necessary for an equation to be correct, not sufficient.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one feature — a wrong numerical constant can hide inside matching units, so homogeneity is necessary but not sufficient.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: use SI base units to check the homogeneity of physical equations

items.prompt: State the factor that the prefix micro represents, and the symbol used for it.
items.canonical_answer: Micro is 10⁻⁶, written with the symbol µ: a time of 3.0 µs is 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ s.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the symbol µ with its factor 10⁻⁶; the prefix attaches directly to the unit symbol, so 3.0 µs is 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ s.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: recall and use the following prefixes and their symbols to indicate decimal submultiples or multiples of both base and derived units: pico (p), nano (n), micro (μ), milli (m), centi (c), deci (d), kilo (k), mega (M), giga (G), tera (T)

items.prompt: A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 98.7 MHz. Calculate the period of one oscillation, giving the answer in seconds and in a suitable prefixed unit.
items.canonical_answer: Convert first: 98.7 MHz is 98.7 × 10⁶ Hz. The period is T = 1 ÷ f, so T = 1 ÷ (98.7 × 10⁶) = 1.013 × 10⁻⁸ s, which is 1.01 × 10⁻⁸ s to three significant figures, or 10.1 ns.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: T = 1 ÷ f with the frequency converted to 98.7 × 10⁶ Hz first — 1 mark for the conversion and the working.
Final answer: 1.01 × 10⁻⁸ s (10.1 ns), with the unit and three significant figures — 1 mark. Dividing by 98.7 without converting leaves the answer six powers of ten out.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: recall and use the following prefixes and their symbols to indicate decimal submultiples or multiples of both base and derived units: pico (p), nano (n), micro (μ), milli (m), centi (c), deci (d), kilo (k), mega (M), giga (G), tera (T)

items.prompt: A copper wire has a cross-sectional area of 0.78 mm². Calculate the area in m², showing the conversion.
items.canonical_answer: The millimetre converts as 10⁻³ m, and the square converts with it: 1 mm² is (10⁻³ m)², which is 10⁻⁶ m². So 0.78 mm² is 0.78 × 10⁻⁶ m², which is 7.8 × 10⁻⁷ m².
marking_guidance: Equation and working: the conversion 1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m², with the factor squared — 1 mark.
Final answer: 7.8 × 10⁻⁷ m², with the unit — 1 mark. An answer of 7.8 × 10⁻³ m² means the factor was not squared, and 7.8 × 10⁻⁵ m² that it was divided instead of multiplied.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: recall and use the following prefixes and their symbols to indicate decimal submultiples or multiples of both base and derived units: pico (p), nano (n), micro (μ), milli (m), centi (c), deci (d), kilo (k), mega (M), giga (G), tera (T)

items.prompt: A laser pulse delivers 45 mJ of energy in a time of 2.0 ns. Calculate the power of the pulse, giving your answer to three significant figures.
items.canonical_answer: Convert both values first: 45 mJ is 45 × 10⁻³ J, which is 0.045 J, and 2.0 ns is 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ s. Then P = E ÷ t, so P = 0.045 ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻⁹) = 2.25 × 10⁷ W, which is 22.5 MW to three significant figures.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: P = E ÷ t with E converted to 0.045 J and t to 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ s — 1 mark for the two conversions and the working.
Final answer: 2.25 × 10⁷ W (22.5 MW), with the unit and three significant figures — 1 mark. A power of ten lost here comes from a prefix left unconverted.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: recall and use the following prefixes and their symbols to indicate decimal submultiples or multiples of both base and derived units: pico (p), nano (n), micro (μ), milli (m), centi (c), deci (d), kilo (k), mega (M), giga (G), tera (T)

items.prompt: Converting an area of 4.0 mm² to m², a learner writes 4.0 × 10⁻³ m². Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The prefix moved with the millimetre but the square did not: the millimetre converts as 10⁻³ m, and the square converts with it, so 1 mm² is (10⁻³ m)², which is 10⁻⁶ m², giving 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ m². The test is whether every value has been converted to base units before substituting, which catches the unsquared factor — the same slip that turns µs into ms or GHz into kHz in a calculation.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named — the conversion factor not squared for an area; the correct idea is (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m², because the test is whether every value is in base units first. Register entry MC-9702-1-09.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger; discriminates misconception register entry MC-9702-1-09.
objective_titles: recall and use the following prefixes and their symbols to indicate decimal submultiples or multiples of both base and derived units: pico (p), nano (n), micro (μ), milli (m), centi (c), deci (d), kilo (k), mega (M), giga (G), tera (T)

items.prompt: State one property of a prefixed unit such as mm² that a conversion to base units must respect.
items.canonical_answer: The prefix is part of the unit, so it is raised to the power with it: mm² converts with 10⁻⁶ to give m², not 10⁻³.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one property — the prefix belongs to the unit and carries the power, so mm² converts with 10⁻⁶; the same point keeps mm³ at 10⁻⁹.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: recall and use the following prefixes and their symbols to indicate decimal submultiples or multiples of both base and derived units: pico (p), nano (n), micro (μ), milli (m), centi (c), deci (d), kilo (k), mega (M), giga (G), tera (T)

items.prompt: State what is meant by a systematic error.
items.canonical_answer: A systematic error shifts every reading of the same measurement by the same amount, or in the same direction. A zero error, where the instrument reads a non-zero value before anything is measured, is a common systematic error.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition — the same shift on every reading, in the same direction, with a zero error as the common example.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: understand and explain the effects of systematic errors (including zero errors) and random errors in measurements

items.prompt: Explain how a zero error affects a set of diameter readings taken with a micrometer, and how the effect differs from random error.
items.canonical_answer: A zero error adds the same offset to every diameter reading: a micrometer that reads 0.02 mm with its jaws closed makes every reading 0.02 mm too large, so the whole set is shifted. Random error, by contrast, scatters readings unpredictably about the mean, and repeating and averaging reduces its effect, because the scatter partly cancels. The zero error survives the averaging, because averaging reduces random error only, so it must be corrected at the source: zero the instrument, or subtract the offset from every reading.
marking_guidance: Mark 1: how the zero error acts — the same offset on every reading, so all readings shift the same way, which is what makes it systematic.
Mark 2: how the effect differs from random error — random scatter is reduced by averaging, whereas the offset survives, so the correction then belongs at the instrument.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: understand and explain the effects of systematic errors (including zero errors) and random errors in measurements

items.prompt: A balance reads 0.05 g with nothing on the pan. A learner measures the mass of a salt sample three times and averages the readings. Explain why the average is still wrong, and what to do.
items.canonical_answer: The balance has a zero error, which is a systematic error: it adds 0.05 g to every reading, so the average of the three readings is 0.05 g too large. Averaging reduces random error only, because random scatter partly cancels; the offset does not. The correction belongs to the instrument: zero the balance, or subtract 0.05 g from every reading before averaging.
marking_guidance: The situation is recognised — a zero error is systematic, so the mean of the three readings is still 0.05 g too large, because averaging reduces random error only — 1 mark. In this case the fix is named: zero the balance or subtract the offset, therefore the correction belongs at the instrument.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: understand and explain the effects of systematic errors (including zero errors) and random errors in measurements

items.prompt: A learner says: take plenty of repeat readings and average, and the zero error on the micrometer will disappear. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: Averaging removes random error, not systematic error. A zero error shifts every reading the same way, so it survives any number of repeats: the mean of ten readings, each 0.02 mm too large, is still 0.02 mm too large. The test is whether the error pushes every reading in the same direction — if it does, repeating cannot help, and the correction is at the instrument: zero it, or subtract the offset from each reading.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named — repeats believed to remove a zero error; in fact averaging reduces random error only, because a systematic error moves every reading the same way. Register entry MC-9702-1-06.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger; discriminates misconception register entry MC-9702-1-06.
objective_titles: understand and explain the effects of systematic errors (including zero errors) and random errors in measurements

items.prompt: State one feature of a random error that repeating and averaging a set of readings exploits.
items.canonical_answer: A random error scatters readings unpredictably about the mean, and the scatter partly cancels when readings are averaged: readings above the mean balance readings below it, so the mean is a better estimate of the true value than a single reading.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one feature — random scatter about the mean, which partly cancels on averaging, so the mean beats a single reading; this works for random error, not for a systematic shift.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: understand and explain the effects of systematic errors (including zero errors) and random errors in measurements

items.prompt: State what is meant by the accuracy of a measured value.
items.canonical_answer: Accuracy is how close a measured value is to the true value.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition — how close the measured value is to the true value.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: understand the distinction between precision and accuracy

items.prompt: State the difference between a precise set of readings and an accurate one.
items.canonical_answer: A precise set of readings agrees closely with each other (small spread, and each reading recorded to a small division); an accurate set is close to the true value. The two are different properties: a set can agree closely and still be shifted from the true value by a systematic error.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the distinction — precise means close agreement between the readings, whereas accurate means close to the true value; both properties can appear separately in one set.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: understand the distinction between precision and accuracy

items.prompt: A learner describes a set of repeat readings as very accurate because they all agree to 0.01 s. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: Close agreement measures precision, not accuracy. The readings agree closely with each other, which is precision; accuracy is closeness to the true value, and a systematic error such as a late-started stopwatch can shift the whole set while the readings still agree. The test is whether the readings could agree closely and all be wrong — here they could, so the set is precise and its accuracy is unproven.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named — precise and accurate used as if they meant the same; in fact agreement between readings is precision, while accuracy is closeness to the true value. Register entry MC-9702-1-05.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger; discriminates misconception register entry MC-9702-1-05.
objective_titles: understand the distinction between precision and accuracy

items.prompt: State one feature of a set of readings that is precise but not accurate.
items.canonical_answer: The readings agree closely with each other while a systematic error shifts the whole set away from the true value, so every reading is wrong in the same way despite the small spread.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one feature — close agreement between readings combined with a systematic shift from the true value; the spread is small, the accuracy is not.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: understand the distinction between precision and accuracy

items.prompt: State the rule for combining the uncertainties of two measured values whose product gives a derived quantity.
items.canonical_answer: For a product (or a quotient), the percentage uncertainties add: the derived quantity's percentage uncertainty is the sum of the two measured values' percentage uncertainties, each being its absolute uncertainty divided by the value itself, multiplied by 100.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the rule given through its meaning — add the percentage uncertainties for a product or quotient, where each is the absolute uncertainty ÷ value × 100; absolute uncertainties add for sums and differences instead.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute or percentage uncertainties

items.prompt: A learner measures two lengths: a = 1.20 m with absolute uncertainty 0.01 m, and b = 0.60 m with absolute uncertainty 0.01 m. Calculate the absolute uncertainty in a + b.
items.canonical_answer: For a sum, the absolute uncertainties add: 0.01 + 0.01 = 0.02 m. So a + b is 1.80 m with an absolute uncertainty of 0.02 m.
marking_guidance: Equation and rule: a sum adds absolute uncertainties — 1 mark for the rule and the substitution.
Final answer: 0.02 m, with the unit — 1 mark. Adding percentage uncertainties here applies the wrong rule to a sum.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute or percentage uncertainties

items.prompt: A minibus travels a straight road at a speed of 20 m s⁻¹ with absolute uncertainty 0.4 m s⁻¹, for a time of 5.0 s with absolute uncertainty 0.1 s. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the distance travelled.
items.canonical_answer: The distance is speed × time, a product, so the percentage uncertainties add. In the speed: 0.4 ÷ 20 = 0.020, so 2.0%. In the time: 0.1 ÷ 5.0 = 0.020, so 2.0%. Adding the fractional forms: 0.020 + 0.020 = 0.040, so the percentage uncertainty in the distance is 4.0% (the distance is 20 × 5.0 = 100 m, so the absolute uncertainty is 4 m).
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: each percentage from absolute uncertainty ÷ value × 100 — 1 mark for both percentages.
Final answer: 4.0% — 1 mark, with the sum shown; adding the absolute uncertainties (0.5 in mixed units) instead applies the rule for a sum.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute or percentage uncertainties

items.prompt: The side of a cube is measured as 0.500 m with a percentage uncertainty of 2.0%. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the volume of the cube, and the absolute uncertainty in that volume.
items.canonical_answer: Volume is the side cubed, and a quantity raised to the power n contributes n times its own percentage uncertainty: the percentage uncertainty in the volume is 3 × 2.0%, which is 6.0%. The volume is 0.125 m³ (0.500³), so the absolute uncertainty is 0.060 × 0.125 = 0.0075 m³.
marking_guidance: Equation and working: V = side³, so the percentage uncertainty triples — 1 mark for the power rule applied.
Final answer: 6.0%, with the absolute uncertainty 0.0075 m³ on V = 0.125 m³ — 1 mark, with the unit on the absolute value; counting the percentage once (2.0%) is the error this calculation avoids.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute or percentage uncertainties

items.prompt: For a distance found from speed × time, a learner adds the two absolute uncertainties to get the uncertainty in the distance. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: Absolute uncertainties add only for sums and differences. A distance from speed × time is a product, so the percentage (or fractional) uncertainties add: each value's absolute uncertainty divided by the value itself, and the two then added. Treating a percentage uncertainty as an absolute one, or adding absolutes for a product, loses track of which rule applies. The test is whether the derived quantity is found by adding or subtracting, or by multiplying or dividing.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named — absolute uncertainties added for a product; in fact products and quotients add percentage uncertainties, because the rule follows the operation that forms the quantity. Register entry MC-9702-1-03.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger; discriminates misconception register entry MC-9702-1-03.
objective_titles: assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute or percentage uncertainties

items.prompt: The area of a circle is found from A = πd²/4. Given a percentage uncertainty of 2.0% in the diameter d, a learner states a percentage uncertainty of 2.0% in the area. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The diameter is squared in the formula, and a quantity raised to the power n contributes n times its own percentage uncertainty: d² contributes twice the percentage uncertainty in d, so the area carries 4.0%, not 2.0%. The test is what power the measured quantity carries in the formula — a square counts twice and a cube three times.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named — the percentage uncertainty of a squared quantity counted once; in fact d² contributes twice d's percentage uncertainty, because the power multiplies it. Register entry MC-9702-1-04.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger; discriminates misconception register entry MC-9702-1-04.
objective_titles: assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute or percentage uncertainties

items.prompt: State one feature of a quantity raised to the power n that its contribution to a percentage uncertainty must reflect.
items.canonical_answer: It contributes n times its own percentage uncertainty: d² counts twice the percentage uncertainty in d, and d³ counts three times.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one feature — the power multiplies the percentage uncertainty, twice for a square and three times for a cube; the exponent in the formula sets the contribution.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute or percentage uncertainties

items.prompt: State what is meant by a vector quantity.
items.canonical_answer: A vector quantity has magnitude and direction: force, displacement, velocity, acceleration, weight and momentum are vectors, while a scalar has magnitude only.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition — magnitude and direction, with at least one correct example (force, displacement, velocity, acceleration, weight, momentum).
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: understand the difference between scalar and vector quantities and give examples of scalar and vector quantities included in the syllabus

items.prompt: State the difference between the distance travelled by a minibus and its displacement.
items.canonical_answer: Distance travelled is a scalar: the total length of the route, with no direction. Displacement is a vector: the distance moved in a stated direction from the starting point, so a taxi that ends where it began has a displacement of zero while its distance travelled is the full length of the route.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the distinction — distance is the scalar total of the route, whereas displacement is the vector from start to end in a stated direction; both ideas are needed to see why a round trip has zero displacement.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: understand the difference between scalar and vector quantities and give examples of scalar and vector quantities included in the syllabus

items.prompt: A learner calls the work done by a force a vector, because a force appears in the equation for work. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The vectors in an equation do not make the quantity a vector. Work, energy, power, pressure and charge are scalars: reversing the direction of the force reverses the sign of the work rather than pointing it anywhere in space, so work is fully described by a magnitude and a sign. The test is whether reversing the direction changes the quantity — a force reversed is a different vector, while a quantity of work keeps its size.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named — work called a vector because vectors appear in its defining equation; in fact work, energy, power, pressure and charge are scalars, because the test is whether reversing the direction changes the quantity. Register entry MC-9702-1-07.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger; discriminates misconception register entry MC-9702-1-07.
objective_titles: understand the difference between scalar and vector quantities and give examples of scalar and vector quantities included in the syllabus

items.prompt: State one property that a vector quantity has and a scalar quantity lacks.
items.canonical_answer: Direction: a vector is fully stated by magnitude and direction together, and reversing its direction changes it; a scalar such as mass or energy has no direction to reverse.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one property — direction, with the reversing test: a reversed vector is a different quantity, whereas a scalar has no direction to reverse.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: understand the difference between scalar and vector quantities and give examples of scalar and vector quantities included in the syllabus

items.prompt: State what is meant by the resultant of two vectors.
items.canonical_answer: The resultant is the single vector with the same effect as the two together: drawn by the triangle method, the second vector starts where the first ends, and the resultant runs from the start of the first to the end of the second.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition — the single vector with the same effect as both, described by the triangle construction (or the parallelogram) as the line from the start of the first to the end of the second.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: add and subtract coplanar vectors

items.prompt: A boat points straight across a river and moves at 3.0 m s⁻¹ relative to the water, while the current flows at 4.0 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to the boat's heading. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the boat's resultant velocity.
items.canonical_answer: The two velocities are perpendicular, so the magnitude comes from R = √(3.0² + 4.0²): R² = 9.0 + 16 = 25, so R = 5.0 m s⁻¹. The direction: tan θ = 4.0 ÷ 3.0 = 1.33, so θ = 53.1° from the boat's heading, towards the downstream side.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: R² = 3.0² + 4.0² for perpendicular vectors, giving R = 5.0 m s⁻¹ — 1 mark for the working.

Final answer: 5.0 m s⁻¹ at 53.1° to the heading (tan θ = 4.0 ÷ 3.0), with the unit and the angle — 1 mark. Adding the magnitudes to get 7.0 m s⁻¹ treats perpendicular vectors as if they pointed the same way.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: add and subtract coplanar vectors

items.prompt: A light aircraft flies at 80 m s⁻¹ relative to the air, heading due north. A wind blows at 30 m s⁻¹ from the north, towards the south. Calculate the aircraft's resultant velocity over the ground.
items.canonical_answer: The two velocities are opposite, so they subtract, or combine by the reverse-vector rule A − B = A + (−B): the resultant is 80 - 30 = 50 m s⁻¹ due north, since the wind acts against the heading.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: opposite directions subtract, or A + (−B) with the wind reversed — 1 mark for the method.
Final answer: 50 m s⁻¹ due north, with the unit and the direction — 1 mark. An answer of 110 m s⁻¹ adds the magnitudes as if the two vectors agreed.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: add and subtract coplanar vectors

items.prompt: Two tractors pull a lorry stuck in sand, their ropes in the same horizontal plane: one with 300 N, the other with 400 N at 60° to the first. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force.
items.canonical_answer: With the angle between the pulls at 60°, R² = P² + Q² + 2PQ cos θ. Substituting: R² = 300² + 400² + 2 × 300 × 400 × cos 60°, and the three terms are 90000, 160000 and 120000, so R² = 370000. R = √370000 = 608 N, so 608 N to three significant figures.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: R² = P² + Q² + 2PQ cos θ, with the terms 90000, 160000 and 120000 — 1 mark for the working.
Final answer: R = 608 N, with the unit and three significant figures — 1 mark. 700 N comes from adding the magnitudes, and 500 N from treating the angle as 90°.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: add and subtract coplanar vectors

items.prompt: State one feature of the triangle method for adding two vectors.
items.canonical_answer: The second vector is drawn starting where the first ends, and the resultant runs from the start of the first to the end of the second — the single vector with the same effect as the two together.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one feature of the construction — head to tail, with the resultant closing the triangle from the start of the first vector to the end of the second.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: add and subtract coplanar vectors

items.prompt:
The table gives the two perpendicular components of a drone's velocity relative to the ground, found from its positions one second apart.

| component | value / m s⁻¹ |
|---|---|
| east | 5.0 |
| north | 12 |

Determine the magnitude and direction of the drone's velocity.
items.canonical_answer: The two components are perpendicular, so the magnitude is R = √(5.0² + 12²): R² = 25 + 144 = 169, so R = 13 m s⁻¹. The direction: tan θ = 12 ÷ 5.0 = 2.4, so θ = 67.4° north of east. The two table values represent this single velocity.
marking_guidance: Reading the table: the values 5.0 m s⁻¹ east and 12 m s⁻¹ north are perpendicular components, so the resultant magnitude follows from R² = 25 + 144 — 1 mark.
The resultant 13 m s⁻¹ at 67.4° north of east gives what the two readings represent as one velocity — 1 mark; the direction is required, so a magnitude alone is half the answer.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: represent a vector as two perpendicular components

items.prompt:
A hiker's displacement at the end of a walk on flat ground is given in the table.

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| displacement magnitude | 1000 m |
| angle to the east direction | 36.9° |

Determine the east and north components of the hiker's displacement.
items.canonical_answer: Resolving along the east direction as the reference: the component alongside the angle is 1000 × cos 36.9° = 1000 × 0.800 = 800 m, and the component opposite the angle, to the north, is 1000 × sin 36.9° = 1000 × 0.601 = 601 m, so 600 m to two significant figures. The two values in the table represent one displacement, and the components recombine to it: 800² + 600² = 1000000, so the magnitude is 1000 m.
marking_guidance: Reading the table: the two values given are a magnitude and an angle, so the components come from 1000 cos 36.9° and 1000 sin 36.9° — 1 mark for both substitutions.

The readings represent one displacement resolved into perpendicular parts: 800 m east and 600 m north, which recombine to the 1000 m in the table — 1 mark; both components with their directions are required.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: represent a vector as two perpendicular components

items.prompt: A crate on a level floor is pulled by a rope at 30° to the horizontal, with a tension of 200 N. Determine the components of the tension along the floor and perpendicular to it.
items.canonical_answer: Along the floor, the component alongside the angle: 200 × cos 30° = 200 × 0.866 = 173.2 N, so 173 N to three significant figures. Perpendicular to the floor, the component opposite the angle: 200 × sin 30° = 200 × 0.500 = 100 N.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: the component alongside the angle is T cos θ and the component opposite it is T sin θ — 1 mark for both substitutions.

Final answer: 173 N along the floor and 100 N perpendicular, with the units and three significant figures — 1 mark. Swapping sine and cosine gives 100 N along the floor, which the alongside/opposite test catches.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: represent a vector as two perpendicular components

items.prompt: Two learners each pull an identical cart with a tension of 100 N: one along the direction of motion, the other at 60° to it. Explain why the carts accelerate differently.
items.canonical_answer: The cart accelerates along its direction of motion, so the component of the tension along that direction decides the acceleration: it is the whole 100 N for the first learner, and 100 × 0.500 = 50 N for the second (the perpendicular component, 87 N, does not accelerate the cart). The second cart accelerates at about half the rate, because the component of the tension along the motion is half as large.
marking_guidance: The situation is analysed — both tensions are 100 N, but the component along the motion is T cos θ, so this case gives 100 N and 50 N — 1 mark.
Therefore the carts accelerate differently, because only the component along the direction of motion drives the cart; the perpendicular component does not — 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: represent a vector as two perpendicular components

items.prompt: Resolving a tension of 200 N at 30° to the horizontal into horizontal and vertical components, a learner writes 200 sin 30° for the horizontal component. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The horizontal component lies alongside the 30° angle, so it is the cosine: 200 cos 30° = 173 N. The sine belongs to the component opposite the angle, the vertical one, which is 100 N. The test is whether the wanted component is next to the angle or opposite it. As a check, set the angle to 0°: the vector is then horizontal, the horizontal component is the whole 200 N, and cos 0° is 1 while sin 0° is 0, so the alongside component must be the cosine.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named — sine and cosine swapped; in fact the component alongside the angle is the cosine, because the test is whether the component is next to the angle or opposite it. Register entry MC-9702-1-08.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger; discriminates misconception register entry MC-9702-1-08.
objective_titles: represent a vector as two perpendicular components

items.prompt: Define the component of a vector along a stated direction.
items.canonical_answer: The component of a vector V along a stated direction is V cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vector and that direction; the component perpendicular to it is V sin θ.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition — V cos θ, with θ the angle between the vector and the stated direction, and the perpendicular component V sin θ named; the equation with its symbols is the definition here.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: represent a vector as two perpendicular components

items.prompt: State one feature of the two perpendicular components of a vector that shows resolving is the reverse of adding.
items.canonical_answer: The components recombine to give the original vector: (V cos θ)² and (V sin θ)² add to V², so the two components, added as perpendicular vectors, rebuild the vector they came from.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: one feature — the components recombine to the original vector, because (V cos θ)² + (V sin θ)² = V²; the two perpendicular parts added by the resultant rule return the starting vector.
items.provenance: Authored for 9702 topic 1 from the topic 1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: represent a vector as two perpendicular components

items.prompt:
Twelve questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. Which prefix represents 10⁻⁹?
A  pico
B  nano
C  micro
D  milli

2. Which quantity is a vector?
A  work
B  power
C  displacement
D  charge

3. A derived quantity is calculated by multiplying two measured values. Which uncertainties are added?
A  the absolute uncertainties
B  the larger absolute uncertainty only
C  the percentage of the larger value only
D  the percentage uncertainties

4. In resolving a vector, V cos θ is the component of V along a reference direction. What is θ?
A  the angle between V and the reference direction
B  the angle between V and the perpendicular to the reference direction
C  the angle between the two components
D  90° minus the angle between V and the reference direction

5. A current is 350 mA. What is it in amperes?
A  3.5 A
B  0.350 A
C  0.0035 A
D  35 A

6. An area is 0.050 mm². What is it in m²?
A  5.0 × 10⁻⁸ m²
B  5.0 × 10⁻⁵ m²
C  5.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m²
D  5.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ m²

7. A distance is calculated as speed × time. The speed is 20 m s⁻¹ with absolute uncertainty 0.4 m s⁻¹; the time is 5.0 s with absolute uncertainty 0.25 s. What is the percentage uncertainty in the distance?
A  2.0%
B  5.0%
C  7.0%
D  0.65%

8. The percentage uncertainty in a measured diameter d is 3.0%. What is the percentage uncertainty in d²?
A  1.5%
B  3.0%
C  6.0%
D  9.0%

9. A force of 60 N acts at 40° to the horizontal. What is the horizontal component?
A  38.6 N
B  60.0 N
C  78.3 N
D  46.0 N

10. Which pair are both scalar quantities?
A  weight and speed
B  power and charge
C  force and energy
D  momentum and mass

11. The horizontal component of a force is 24 N and the vertical component is 32 N. What is the magnitude of the force?
A  40 N
B  56 N
C  8.0 N
D  768 N

12. A signal has a frequency of 5.0 GHz. What is its period?
A  0.20 µs
B  2.0 ns
C  0.20 ms
D  0.20 ns
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 C, 3 D, 4 A, 5 B, 6 A, 7 C, 8 C, 9 D, 10 B, 11 A, 12 D.
1. Nano is 10⁻⁹ (B); A is pico (10⁻¹²), C is micro (10⁻⁶) and D is milli (10⁻³) — each a neighbouring power of ten.
2. Displacement has magnitude and direction (C); work, power and charge are scalars, the error of trusting the vectors in a defining equation.
3. A product adds percentage uncertainties (D); A applies the rule for sums and differences, and B and C keep only one value's uncertainty.
4. θ is the angle between the vector and the reference direction (A); B and D use the complementary angle, and C confuses the angle between the components with the angle to the reference.
5. Milli is 10⁻³, so 350 mA is 0.350 A (B); A slips a factor of 1000 up, D a factor of 100 up, and C two factors down.
6. The millimetre and the square both convert: 0.050 mm² is 0.050 × 10⁻⁶ m², which is 5.0 × 10⁻⁸ m² (A); B leaves the factor unsquared (10⁻³), C uses the cubic factor (10⁻⁹), and D squares the converted factor a second time.
7. The percentages: 0.4 ÷ 20 = 0.020 (2.0%) and 0.25 ÷ 5.0 = 0.050 (5.0%), and 2.0% + 5.0% = 7.0% (C); A counts only the speed's percentage, B only the time's, and D adds the absolute uncertainties (0.4 + 0.25 = 0.65) as a fraction of the distance (20 × 5.0 = 100 m), which is the sum rule applied to a product.
8. A squared quantity carries twice the percentage: 2 × 3.0%, which is 6.0% (C); B counts it once, A halves it, and D applies the cube rule.
9. The horizontal component lies alongside the angle: 60 × 0.766 = 46.0 N (D); A swaps sine for cosine (60 × 0.643 = 38.6 N), B ignores the angle, and C divides by cos 40° instead of multiplying (60 ÷ 0.766 = 78.3 N).
10. Power and charge are both scalars (B); A, C and D each pair a scalar with a vector — weight, force and momentum respectively.
11. The components are perpendicular, so the magnitude is √(24² + 32²) = √1600 = 40 N (A); B adds the magnitudes (24 + 32 = 56 N), C subtracts them, and D multiplies them.
12. T = 1 ÷ (5.0 × 10⁹) = 0.20 × 10⁻⁹ s, which is 0.20 ns (D); A, B and C each slip a power of ten in the prefix.
marking_guidance: The key: one mark per question, twelve in total; the correct option for each question is listed, and the answer explains each one.

Every distractor is a named error: a neighbouring prefix (a power of ten slipped), a conversion factor not squared, absolute and percentage uncertainties confused, a power's contribution counted once, sine and cosine swapped, magnitudes added for perpendicular vectors, and a scalar called a vector — each wrong option traces to one of these.

items.prompt:
A learner checks the capacity of a rectangular water tank on a farm near Otjiwarongo. She measures the length, width and depth with a tape: length 1.20 m, width 0.750 m, depth 0.500 m. Her tape has a permanent zero error: it reads 0.02 m before any length is measured.

(a) State what is meant by a reasonable estimate. [1]
(b) Each of her three measurements carries an absolute uncertainty of 0.02 m. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the volume of the tank. [3]
(c) Explain why taking several readings of the length and averaging does not remove the effect of the zero error. [2]
(d) Calculate the volume of the tank. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) A reasonable estimate states a magnitude with its unit, judged without measuring directly, and is expected to lie within about a power of ten of the actual value.
(b) Volume is a product of the three lengths, so the percentage uncertainties add. In the length: 0.02 ÷ 1.20 = 0.0167, so 1.7%. In the width: 0.02 ÷ 0.750 = 0.0267, so 2.7%. In the depth: 0.02 ÷ 0.500 = 0.040, so 4.0%. The percentage uncertainty in the volume is 1.7% + 2.7% + 4.0% = 8.4%.
(c) The zero error is a systematic error: it shifts every reading of the length by the same 0.02 m, in the same direction. Repeating and averaging reduces the effect of random error only, because random scatter partly cancels; the offset survives any number of repeats, so the correction belongs at the instrument — zero the tape, or subtract 0.02 m from every reading before use.
(d) V = l × w × d, so 1.20 × 0.750 = 0.900, and 0.900 × 0.500 = 0.450 m³. The volume is 0.450 m³ to three significant figures.
marking_guidance: Part (a): 1 mark for the definition — a magnitude with its unit, judged without measuring directly, expected within about a power of ten of the actual value.

Part (b): 1 mark for each percentage (0.02 ÷ 1.20, 0.02 ÷ 0.750 and 0.02 ÷ 0.500, each × 100) and 1 mark for the sum 8.4%; the equation is percentage uncertainty = absolute ÷ value × 100, added across a product.

Part (c): 1 mark for the reason — a zero error is systematic and shifts every reading the same way, so averaging reduces random error only; 1 mark for the point that the correction belongs at the instrument.
Part (d): 1 mark for the substitution into V = l × w × d, 1 mark for the answer 0.450 m³ with its unit and three significant figures.

objective_titles: make reasonable estimates of physical quantities included within the syllabus
understand and explain the effects of systematic errors (including zero errors) and random errors in measurements
assess the uncertainty in a derived quantity by simple addition of absolute or percentage uncertainties

items.prompt:
A learner measures the diameter of a wire with a micrometer and records d = 0.32 mm, with an absolute uncertainty of 0.01 mm. The cross-sectional area of the wire is A = πd²/4.
Calculate the area in m² and the absolute uncertainty in the area, giving each answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.
items.canonical_answer:
Convert both values to base units first: d = 0.32 mm = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ m, and the absolute uncertainty is 0.01 mm = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ m.
The area: A = πd²/4. Carrying the working, d² = (3.2 × 10⁻⁴)² = 1.024 × 10⁻⁷ m², so A = 3.1416 × 1.024 × 10⁻⁷ ÷ 4 = 8.04 × 10⁻⁸ m².
The percentage uncertainty in the diameter: 0.01 ÷ 0.32 = 0.031, so 3.1% (the same result comes from 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 3.2 × 10⁻⁴, because converting both to metres leaves the ratio unchanged).
The area goes as d², so it carries twice: 2 × 3.1%, which is 6.2%.
The absolute uncertainty in the area: 0.062 × 8.04 = 0.498, so 5.0 × 10⁻⁹ m².
The diameter is given to two significant figures, so the area is quoted as A = (8.0 ± 0.5) × 10⁻⁸ m², that is 8.0 × 10⁻⁸ m² with an absolute uncertainty of 5.0 × 10⁻⁹ m².
marking_guidance: Equation: A = πd²/4 with the diameter converted to 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ m before anything else — 1 mark for the conversion.
Substitution and working: d² = 1.024 × 10⁻⁷ m², so A = 8.04 × 10⁻⁸ m² — 1 mark; the percentage uncertainty in d as 0.01 ÷ 0.32 × 100 = 3.1% — 1 mark.
Answer: the percentage doubled for d² (6.2%) and the absolute uncertainty 5.0 × 10⁻⁹ m², with the units and the significant figures justified against the two significant figures in d — 2 marks.
